items.title: Anti-Black Racism Was a Factor in Son's Fatal Shooting by Police, Mississauga Mother Tells Inquest
items.summary: According to insauga.com, Ann-Marie White, the mother of Jamal Francique, testified at a coroner's inquest that she believes anti-Black racism played a role in her son's fatal shooting by Peel police nearly seven years ago. White said officers who testified could recall their training on use of force and firearms but not on anti-Black racism, leaving her to question whether there was a genuine effort to address bias. She said she remains troubled that about 25 minutes passed before her son got medical help after he was shot. White, the final witness at the inquest, said police resorted to an elaborate and botched plan to arrest Francique on Jan. 7, 2020, based on unconfirmed allegations. Police secretly surveilled Francique for days after a Crime Stoppers tip alleged he had drugs and a gun, but found nothing and arrested him instead for an alleged bail breach.

items.title: Mississauga Pushes Back Celebration Square Rink Opening to Dec. 4 Amid Mild Weather
items.summary: According to the City of Mississauga, unseasonably mild weather has pushed back the opening of the outdoor skating rink at Celebration Square in the downtown core. The rink typically opens alongside the city's annual Christmas tree lighting ceremony, which went ahead as scheduled last Saturday along with the Santa Claus parade, but ice making could not begin on schedule this year. City spokesperson Irene McCutcheon told insauga.com that staff usually start making ice in mid-November so the rink is ready for the tree lighting, but mild temperatures made that impossible this time. She said crews are now targeting a Dec. 4 opening, though the weather will decide when the ice is ready. The same mild conditions cut the rink's run short back in March, when it closed on March 7. Officials have said a historic El Nino pattern could bring milder temperatures to the region this winter.

items.title: Owner's Objections Fail to Stop Heritage Designation for Mississauga Chinese Centre
items.summary: According to a report before Mississauga's Heritage Advisory Committee, the Mississauga Chinese Centre at 888 Dundas St. has been approved for a heritage designation despite opposition from the owner. The centre was built in the 1980s by Hong Kong investors and features replica Chinese landmarks, including a nine dragon wall and an entry gate, and was added to the city's Heritage Register in 1989. The committee considered the designation at its Nov. 24 meeting, where lawyer Rodney Gill, speaking for the owner, argued the property no longer meets the criteria. Through a translator, the owner said the designation would delay repairs and leave the business facing costlier renovations, and strongly opposed the move. Gill told the committee the staff report was completed about a year ago and the site has changed since, with statues removed and the fortress structure altered.

items.title: Eight Tower Cranes Rise Over Mississauga as Canada's Biggest Hospital Takes Shape
items.summary: According to Trillium Health Partners, eight tower cranes are working on what is expected to be the biggest hospital in Canada when it opens in 2034. The tallest crane rises about 146 metres, roughly a quarter the height of Toronto's CN Tower, as crews build the Peter Gilgan Mississauga Hospital on the site of the current Mississauga Hospital. The network said this week the work can generate noise, and crews have taken steps to limit the impact on neighbours, including a sound wall and quieter equipment. Trillium Health Partners said residents may still hear crane horns, since operators sound them to warn workers below when a load is lifted overhead. The network also runs Credit Valley Hospital and Etobicoke's Queensway Health Centre, and says the new tower will include the Shah Family Hospital for Women and Children, Ontario's first such facility.

items.title: Bank of Canada Partners With Peel Schools to Teach Students Real-World Financial Skills
items.summary: According to the Peel District School Board, a new partnership with the Bank of Canada Museum launched Thursday to teach real-world financial skills to students in Mississauga and Brampton. About 250 students in Grades 10 through 12 took part in the first workshops, covering the central bank's role, interest rate decisions, economic trends and financial literacy. The board says the year-long program gives students exposure to careers in economics, research, financial markets and policy-making. The initiative comes as updated rules take effect this year, requiring students to score at least 70 per cent on financial literacy modules in the Grade 10 Career Studies course, worth 5 per cent of their final grade. The board says the requirement builds on lessons taught from Grades 1 through 9. The province says students must also learn to budget and meet the 70 per cent threshold to graduate.

items.title: Francique Was Rushing to See His Dying Grandfather, Not Breaching Bail, Mother Tells Inquest
items.summary: According to Mississauga.com, Ann-Marie White testified at a coroner's inquest that her son Jamal Francique left home the night he was fatally shot by police not to breach his bail conditions, but to see his dying grandfather. White said she learned from Francique's father, Derek, that Derek's own father had a medical emergency on the evening of Jan. 7, 2020, and that Derek had called Jamal to tell him. She told the inquest her son was leaving to say goodbye to his grandfather and believed he qualified for a house arrest exception for family medical emergencies, but he never made it. Francique, a 28 year old father of two, was on bail from 2018 drug and gun charges when plainclothes officers from a vice narcotics unit tried to arrest him at his Southampton Drive townhouse over an alleged bail breach. White told the inquest police acted as judge, jury and executioner in that parking lot.

items.title: Ontario to Require Licences and Insurance for Motorcycle-Style E-Bikes Next May
items.summary: According to insauga.com, Ontario Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria announced that drivers of motorcycle-style e-bikes will need a driver's licence, registration and insurance to operate on provincial roads starting next May. Sarkaria said vehicles that look like e-bikes but function more like motorcycles pose serious risks to pedestrians, cyclists, riders and drivers. Under the new definition, a true e-bike must have a bicycle-style frame, operable pedals and a motor-assisted top speed of 32 km/h, with anything faster banned from bike lanes and subject to the new licensing rules. The province said penalties will include fines of up to $2,500 and vehicle impoundment. Mississauga Mayor Alvin Tedjo welcomed the change, saying residents have called for stronger e-bike safety measures for years as the city grapples with danger on its streets from some riders.

items.title: Port Credit's 130-Year-Old United Church Could Become City-Owned Event Venue
items.summary: According to insauga.com, the City of Mississauga is in the process of buying a more than 130-year-old United Church property at 151 Lakeshore Rd. W. in Port Credit, which has been listed for sale for nearly six months. Then-Mayor Carolyn Parrish announced in July that the city planned to turn the building into an event venue and a permanent home for the Canada Virtuoso Ensemble. The church, most recently known as Christ First United Church, amalgamated with the Clarkson Christ First United Church on Mazo Crescent in 2019 and moved its regular services there the same year. A Spanish-language congregation currently holds services in the Port Credit building on typical Sundays, according to a church spokesperson. The congregation is also planning a Candlelight Service at the Port Credit church in December, the spokesperson said.

items.title: UTM Intern's New Series Traces Mississauga's Ties to Japanese Canadian Internment
items.summary: According to Modern Mississauga Media, a new four-part series is tracing the connections between Mississauga and the internment of Japanese Canadians during the Second World War. The series, titled A Path to Mississauga, was researched and written by Darrion Singh, a University of Toronto Mississauga graduate who completed a Historical Studies internship with Heritage Mississauga from September 2025 to March 2026. Singh's project revisits how Canada declared war on Japan on Dec. 7, 1941, after the attack on Pearl Harbor, and how Ottawa later invoked the War Measures Act to expel Japanese Canadians from British Columbia by early 1942. The outlet reports Singh credits Heritage Mississauga and University of Toronto Mississauga staff for guiding the internship. The series will explore how Japanese Canadians remember this history and its ties to the Mississauga area, Singh says.

items.title: Peel Inspectors Shut Down a Dundas Street Restaurant and Bakery
items.summary: According to Peel Public Health, inspectors temporarily closed a Mississauga restaurant and bakery during a routine food safety inspection. Revrea's Grill & Bakeshop, located at 1057 Dundas St., was ordered to close when it was inspected on Nov. 25, the health unit says. Peel Public Health routinely checks local restaurants, cocktail bars, bakeries and takeout establishments to ensure compliance with the Health Protection and Promotion Act. A green pass indicates a business is meeting food safety and operational standards, according to the region of Peel. The health unit did not specify in its public summary what led inspectors to order the closure.
